solution.concept_anchor: Non-justiciability vs. legal irrelevance of FDs
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is a strong distractor because students conflate 'no enforcement mechanism' with 'complete constitutional irrelevance', missing courts' interpretive use of FDs.
elimination_logic: Eliminate options claiming FDs can be enforced by writs under Article 32 or 226 — Part IVA contains no enforcement clause equivalent to Article 32.
Eliminate options equating FDs' non-justiciability with total legal irrelevance — courts use FDs as interpretive tools.
Retain the option distinguishing non-justiciability from interpretive irrelevance — this reflects settled judicial practice.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here exploits the common conflation of 'non-justiciable' with 'legally irrelevant'. A student who has merely read that FDs are non-enforceable may mark option d (completely irrelevant to courts) as correct. The precise knowledge required is that while no writ lies to enforce a FD, courts actively invoke FDs under the harmonious construction principle to resolve ambiguity in statutes and constitutional provisions — making them legally significant even without an enforcement mechanism.
solution.final_explanation:
Part IVA of the Constitution, which contains Fundamental Duties (Article 51A), lacks any enforcement clause comparable to Article 32 (which makes Fundamental Rights justiciable) or Article 226 (High Court writs). This makes FDs non-justiciable in the primary sense — no citizen can file a writ to enforce them.

• Option (a): Incorrect. FDs are non-justiciable; Article 32 applies exclusively to Part III Fundamental Rights.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Parliament can legislate to give effect to FDs using its ordinary legislative competence — no special article is required or exists for this purpose.
• Option (c): Correct. While FDs are non-justiciable, courts consistently use them as interpretive guides — a harmonious construction tool — to resolve ambiguity in statutes and constitutional provisions.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Non-justiciability does not mean legal irrelevance; the AIIMS Students Union case (2002) explicitly called FDs 'constitutional obligations' relevant to interpretation.

Value Addition:
• Article 51A uses 'It shall be the duty of every citizen' — obligatory language without an enforcement clause.
• The distinction between non-justiciable DPSPs and non-justiciable FDs: DPSPs bind the State; FDs bind citizens.
• Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) illustrates courts examining FDs even when ultimately ruling in favour of Fundamental Rights.

solution.concept_anchor: Swaran Singh Committee recommendations vs. enacted provisions

statement_analysis.statement: The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended that violation of Fundamental Duties should attract penal consequences, and this recommendation was incorporated into the 42nd Constitutional Amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: The Committee did recommend penal consequences for FD violations, but this was NOT incorporated into the 42nd Amendment — the final constitutional text omitted this provision.

statement_analysis.statement: The Swaran Singh Committee originally recommended ten Fundamental Duties, all of which were added by the 42nd Amendment, while the 86th Amendment (2002) added the eleventh duty under Article 51A(k).
statement_analysis.reason: The Committee recommended 10 duties; the 42nd Amendment enacted 10 duties; the 86th Amendment added the 11th duty — the parent/guardian duty to provide education to children aged 6–14 years.

statement_analysis.statement: The Swaran Singh Committee recommended that Parliament should be explicitly mandated by the Constitution to enact laws enforcing Fundamental Duties, but the constitutional text does not include such a mandate.
statement_analysis.reason: The Committee envisioned parliamentary enforceability as a constitutional mandate, but the 42nd Amendment's final text did not include any such explicit direction to Parliament.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because students who know Statement 2 is correct may assume Statement 1 is also correct (since penal consequences were recommended), missing the critical distinction that the recommendation was not enacted.
elimination_logic: Eliminate any option that includes Statement 1 — the penal consequences recommendation was made by the Committee but was deliberately excluded from the 42nd Amendment's text.
Confirm Statement 2 as correct — the 42nd Amendment added 10 duties (matching the Committee's recommendation) and the 86th Amendment added the 11th.
Confirm Statement 3 as correct — the Committee's intent for enforceable parliamentary mandate was diluted in the final constitutional text.
The only option containing Statements 2 and 3 but not Statement 1 is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the partial truth in Statement 1. Students know the Committee recommended penal consequences — which is correct — but the crucial second half (that this was incorporated) is false. The seductive logic is: 'the recommendation existed, therefore it was implemented.' This partial-truth distractor catches students who remember the Committee's recommendation but have not specifically noted that it was excluded from the final text.
solution.final_explanation:
The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) was constituted to examine whether Fundamental Duties should be added to the Constitution. Its recommendations were partially accepted and partially rejected during the 42nd Amendment process.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Committee did recommend penal consequences for FD violations, but this recommendation was consciously omitted from the 42nd Amendment (1976). The enacted FDs carry no penal clause within the Constitution itself.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Committee recommended 10 duties; the 42nd Amendment added exactly 10 duties. The 86th Amendment (2002) subsequently added the 11th duty — Article 51A(k) — placing an obligation on parents/guardians to provide education to children between 6 and 14 years.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Committee envisioned that Parliament would be constitutionally mandated to legislate enforcement mechanisms for FDs, but no such explicit mandate appears in Article 51A or elsewhere in Part IVA.

Value Addition:
• The gap between the Committee's intent and the enacted text is a recurring UPSC theme — particularly regarding penal enforceability.
• Article 51A(k) is the only FD added after the original 42nd Amendment insertion.
• The absence of a 'Parliament shall' clause for FDs contrasts with Article 35, which explicitly empowers Parliament to make laws regarding certain Fundamental Rights.

concepts_used: Parliamentary Power to Enforce Fundamental Duties via Legislation

solution.concept_anchor: No Article 35 equivalent for FD enforcement by Parliament

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament derives its power to legislate for enforcing Fundamental Duties from a specific constitutional article in Part IVA, analogous to Article 35 which grants Parliament exclusive power over certain Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: No such specific article exists in Part IVA. Parliament enforces FDs through its ordinary legislative competence under the Union and Concurrent Lists — not through any dedicated constitutional provision.

statement_analysis.statement: The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, and the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, are among the statutes that give effect to specific Fundamental Duties, even though both statutes predate the insertion of Fundamental Duties by the 42nd Amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Acts predate the 42nd Amendment (1976). FDs provided constitutional backing to these laws retrospectively — the laws derive enforcement power from legislative competence, not from Article 51A.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because students aware of pre-existing statutes may incorrectly conclude Statement 2 is wrong (assuming FDs must precede implementing legislation), thus selecting the wrong 'incorrect' statement.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1 — there is no Article in Part IVA giving Parliament exclusive or special power to legislate for FDs; this is a fabricated provision. Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Check Statement 2 — both the Wildlife Protection Act (1972) and Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971) do predate the 42nd Amendment (1976) but are recognised as implementing FD obligations retrospectively. Statement 2 is correct.
The question asks which is NOT correct — only Statement 1 qualifies, making (a) the answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the natural assumption that since Article 35 empowers Parliament to legislate for Fundamental Rights, a parallel provision must exist for Fundamental Duties. This plausible-fabrication distractor sounds authoritative — students familiar with Article 35's structure may accept a similar article for FDs without question. The precise knowledge required is the absence of any such dedicated article in Part IVA.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliament's authority to legislate on matters relating to Fundamental Duties flows from its ordinary legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule — not from any dedicated article within Part IVA.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect (NOT correct): This is a fabricated provision. Article 35 grants Parliament specific exclusive power over certain Fundamental Rights, but no equivalent article exists for Fundamental Duties in Part IVA. Parliament relies on entries in the Union and Concurrent Lists to enact FD-implementing legislation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Both the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971) and the Wildlife Protection Act (1972) predate the 42nd Amendment (1976). When FDs were inserted, these laws acquired constitutional backing retrospectively — the doctrine of 'constitutional backing' enhances their legitimacy without altering their legislative source of power.

Value Addition:
• RTE Act 2009 is a more recent example — it implements Article 51A(k) though its direct constitutional anchor is Article 21A.
• The absence of an Article 35-equivalent for FDs means FD-implementing laws face ordinary legislative scrutiny, not any enhanced judicial deference.
• Laws enforcing FDs still must conform to Fundamental Rights — constitutional backing does not make them immune to challenge.

solution.concept_anchor: FDs aid reasonable restriction test, not override FRs
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because both A and R are individually correct, leading students to assume causal connection without examining whether R actually explains A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Courts do use Fundamental Duties to justify reasonable restrictions on Fundamental Rights under Article 19(2)-(6), upholding laws that might otherwise seem disproportionate.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Fundamental Duties apply exclusively to citizens; the language of Article 51A is 'every citizen', unlike Articles 14, 20, and 21 which use 'person'.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The exclusive applicability of FDs to citizens does not explain why courts use FDs to justify reasonable restrictions on Article 19 rights. The causal mechanism for A is that FDs reflect constitutional values that inform the public order/morality/decency standards under Article 19(2)-(6), not the citizen-exclusivity of FDs.
Both correct but R does not explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is a reversed-causation design where both A and R are independently true, but R has no logical or causal relationship to A. Students who verify each statement's factual accuracy and find both correct often default to option (a) without testing the causal link. The actual mechanism by which FDs aid the reasonable restriction test is through their reflection of constitutional values, not through their limited applicability to citizens.
solution.final_explanation:
Fundamental Duties serve as a significant aid when courts examine the validity of laws restricting Fundamental Rights — particularly Article 19 freedoms — under the reasonable restriction framework.

Assertion (A): Correct. Courts have invoked FDs to support laws that impose restrictions on Article 19 rights. For instance, laws protecting national symbols or the environment gain constitutional weight from FDs like 51A(a) and 51A(g), supporting the argument that restrictions serve constitutionally recognised values of public order, morality, and national interest.

Reason (R): Correct. Article 51A uses the phrase 'every citizen' — a deliberate distinction from Articles 14, 20, and 21, which protect 'persons'. FDs thus exclude corporations, foreign nationals, and other legal entities.

Causal Relationship: R does NOT explain A. The reason courts use FDs in the reasonable restriction analysis is that FDs embody constitutional values recognised by the framers — not because FDs are limited to citizens. The citizen-exclusivity of FDs is an independent structural feature with no bearing on their use in the Article 19 balancing exercise.

Value Addition:
• Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986): SC examined FD 51A(a) while ultimately holding compelled singing violates Article 19.
• Ranganatha Misra Commission noted FDs can justify restrictions under Article 19(2)-(6).
• FDs cannot override FRs — they assist in determining the proportionality and legitimacy of restrictions, not in extinguishing rights.

solution.concept_anchor: Landmark cases and FD-related judicial holdings
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because it places Bijoe Emmanuel correctly but swaps the AIIMS Students Union and MC Mehta holdings, which both relate to non-enforcement of FDs directly but through different mechanisms.
elimination_logic: Anchor on AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2002): SC held FDs are 'constitutional obligations' relevant to interpretation but not enforceable by writ — matches with description 3.

Anchor on Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986): Court ruled that compelling students to sing the national anthem violates Article 19 — matches with description 2 (FR prevails, compulsion invalid).
MC Mehta v. Union of India: FD 51A(g) used to support expansive Article 21 interpretation for right to clean environment — matches with description 1.
Chandra Bhavan Boarding v. State of Mysore: SC observed rights and duties are correlative and inseparable — matches description 4. This gives option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates between AIIMS Students Union and MC Mehta — both cases involve non-enforcement of FDs directly, but through very different holdings. Students who conflate 'FD used in PIL context' (Mehta) with 'FD as constitutional obligation for interpretation' (AIIMS) will mismatch these two. The Bijoe Emmanuel placement is also a potential trap since students may associate it with FD enforcement rather than recognising that the SC actually ruled against compulsion.
solution.final_explanation:
Indian courts have engaged with Fundamental Duties across multiple landmark judgments, each establishing a distinct principle about their legal character.

• A–1 (MC Mehta v. Union of India): Correct match. The Court used FD 51A(g) (protect environment) to justify an expansive reading of Article 21, recognising a right to clean environment — the enforcement mechanism was Article 21/32, not FD directly.
• B–2 (Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala, 1986): Correct match. The SC ruled that compelling students to sing the national anthem violates their rights under Article 19(1)(a), even while examining FD 51A(a). FDs do not override Fundamental Rights.
• C–3 (AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS, 2002): Correct match. The Court explicitly held that FDs are not enforceable by writ but constitute 'constitutional obligations' that courts consider while interpreting provisions — the definitive ruling on FD interpretive status.
• D–4 (Chandra Bhavan Boarding v. State of Mysore): Correct match. The SC articulated the correlative theory — rights and duties are inseparable in a democratic framework — a foundational statement for the jurisprudential argument for FD enforceability.

Value Addition:
• AIIMS Students Union (2002) is the most cited case on FD non-justiciability.
• Bijoe Emmanuel is frequently misread as endorsing FD enforcement — it actually limits FD over FR.
• The correlative theory from Chandra Bhavan remains jurisprudential argument, not settled law.

concepts_used: Relationship Between Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles of State Policy

solution.concept_anchor: DPSPs bind State; FDs bind citizens — key distinction

statement_analysis.statement: Directive Principles of State Policy and Fundamental Duties are both non-justiciable, but they differ in that DPSPs impose obligations on the State while Fundamental Duties impose obligations on citizens.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the foundational structural distinction — DPSPs (Part IV) direct State action; FDs (Part IVA) direct citizen conduct. Both lack direct judicial enforcement.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(g), which requires citizens to protect the natural environment, and Article 48A, which directs the State to protect and improve the environment, impose identical legal obligations on both citizens and the State respectively and are therefore jointly enforceable through the same writ petition.
statement_analysis.reason: While both provisions address environmental protection and are complementary in spirit, neither is directly enforceable by writ — Article 48A (DPSP) and Article 51A(g) (FD) both lack enforcement clauses. Courts enforce environmental rights through Article 21, not through these provisions jointly.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is correct and students who are familiar with the DPSP-FD distinction may not carefully examine Statement 2's false claim of 'joint enforceability'.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is a well-established constitutional distinction — DPSPs bind the State, FDs bind citizens, both non-justiciable. Mark as correct.

Statement 2 contains a conflation error — it merges two non-justiciable provisions and falsely claims they are 'jointly enforceable' by writ. Neither Article 48A nor Article 51A(g) is directly writ-enforceable. Mark as incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in Statement 2 merges two real provisions (48A and 51A(g)) that genuinely mirror each other and falsely implies that their thematic overlap creates joint enforceability. Students who know both provisions address environmental protection may assume the joint enforceability claim follows logically, missing the critical point that neither is independently writ-enforceable.
solution.final_explanation:
The DPSP-FD relationship is a high-frequency UPSC theme, particularly the distinction in obligation-bearers.

• Statement 1 — Correct: DPSPs (Part IV) impose obligations on the State in governance and policy-making; FDs (Part IVA) impose obligations on every citizen in civic conduct. Both are non-justiciable, but their subjects of obligation are categorically different — a distinction courts and constitutional scholars consistently emphasise.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 48A (DPSP) and Article 51A(g) (FD) do address the same subject — environmental protection — and the Verma Committee noted this as a 'complementary framework'. However, joint enforceability by writ is incorrect. Courts enforce the right to a clean environment through Article 21, not through these provisions directly, and no writ petition can be founded on Article 48A or 51A(g) alone.

Value Addition:
• The Article 48A / Article 51A(g) pairing is the most cited example of DPSP-FD complementarity.
• Verma Committee (1999) described DPSPs and FDs together as a 'complementary framework of national obligations'.
• In MC Mehta cases, Article 21 (not Article 48A or 51A(g)) was the judicial enforcement vehicle for environmental rights.

solution.concept_anchor: Verma Committee 1999 — operationalisation not justiciability
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students aware of the Committee's activist recommendations may assume it pushed for justiciability, conflating 'operationalisation' with 'legal enforcement'.
elimination_logic: Eliminate options suggesting the Verma Committee recommended making FDs justiciable — the Committee's mandate and findings were confined to identifying existing implementing laws and recommending awareness, not new enforcement machinery.
Eliminate options claiming the Committee recommended a new constitutional amendment — it recommended operationalising the existing framework.
The correct answer identifies awareness campaigns and existing law mapping as the Committee's primary recommendations.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap is embedded in options that extend the Committee's recommendation from 'operationalisation within the existing non-justiciable framework' to 'making FDs justiciable'. Students who remember the Committee as pro-enforcement may assume it recommended justiciability, but its actual finding was that existing laws already implemented FDs — the gap was awareness, not legal enforceability.
solution.final_explanation:
The Justice J.S. Verma Committee was appointed in 1999 by the Ministry of Human Resource Development to examine how Fundamental Duties were being implemented and what further steps could be taken.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The Committee did not recommend making FDs justiciable. Its conclusions worked entirely within the non-justiciable framework.
• Option (b): Correct. The Committee's key finding was that several laws already implemented FDs, but citizens and enforcement authorities were largely unaware of this connection. It recommended awareness campaigns and incorporation of FDs in school curricula — not new enforcement mechanisms.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The Committee did not recommend a constitutional amendment to insert enforcement provisions.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The Committee did not recommend parliamentary legislation specifically mandating punishments for FD violations — that was the rejected Swaran Singh Committee recommendation.

Value Addition:
• The Verma Committee is distinct from the Swaran Singh Committee — Swaran Singh (1976) recommended enforceability; Verma (1999) recommended awareness.
• NCF (National Curriculum Framework) incorporates FD awareness partly pursuant to Verma Committee recommendations.
• The Committee's approach reflects a 'soft enforcement' philosophy — civic education over legal compulsion.

concepts_used: Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k) and Right to Education (86th Amendment, 2002)

solution.concept_anchor: Article 51A(k) vs Article 21A — duty unenforceable, right enforceable

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(k) imposes a Fundamental Duty on parents and guardians to provide educational opportunities to their children between the ages of 6 and 14 years, and this duty is directly enforceable through a writ petition.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 51A(k) is a Fundamental Duty — it is not directly enforceable through writ. The enforceable provision is Article 21A (Right to Education), not the corresponding duty.

statement_analysis.statement: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, operationalises both Article 21A (Right to Education) and the spirit of Article 51A(k), though enforcement flows from the right under Article 21A and not from the duty under Article 51A(k).
statement_analysis.reason: The RTE Act 2009 implements the constitutional mandate of Article 21A and reflects the intent of Article 51A(k), but the judicial enforcement vehicle is Article 21A — the non-justiciable FD provides normative backing without itself being enforceable.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(k) is unique among Fundamental Duties in that it is the only duty that has a directly corresponding enforceable Fundamental Right — Article 21A — within the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: No other FD has a directly paired, constitutionally enforceable right. The Article 51A(k)–Article 21A pairing is constitutionally unique.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (1 and 3 only) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 3 as true but mistakenly believe the duty in 51A(k) is enforceable via writ (since the right exists) will pair it with Statement 1.
elimination_logic: Eliminate Statement 1 — Article 51A(k) is a Fundamental Duty in Part IVA; no writ lies to enforce it directly regardless of the existence of a corresponding right under Article 21A.
Confirm Statement 2 — RTE Act 2009 operationalises Article 21A primarily; 51A(k) provides normative backing. The enforcement mechanism is the right, not the duty. Statement 2 is correct.
Confirm Statement 3 — the 51A(k)/21A pairing is constitutionally unique; no other FD has a paired enforceable constitutional right. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 correct, Statement 1 incorrect — answer is (d) 2 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 1 exploits the association between Article 51A(k) and the enforceable Article 21A. Students reason: 'the right is enforceable, the duty mirrors the right, therefore the duty must also be enforceable.' This conflation is the error — enforceability flows from the right (Article 21A), not from the duty (51A(k)). The duty remains non-justiciable even though it has a directly corresponding enforceable right.
solution.final_explanation:
The 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) is significant for simultaneously inserting Article 21A (Right to Education) and Article 51A(k) (parent/guardian duty) — creating a unique rights-duties symmetry within the Constitution.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 51A(k) is a Fundamental Duty situated in Part IVA, which contains no enforcement clause. A writ petition cannot be filed to enforce it. The enforceable obligation on the State flows from Article 21A, not from 51A(k).
• Statement 2 — Correct: The RTE Act 2009 operationalises Article 21A's mandate and implicitly reflects Article 51A(k)'s spirit, but judicial enforcement uses Article 21A as the constitutional hook, not 51A(k).
• Statement 3 — Correct: Among all eleven Fundamental Duties, only Article 51A(k) has a directly corresponding enforceable constitutional right (Article 21A). No other FD enjoys this structural symmetry.

Value Addition:
• The age bracket in both Article 21A and Article 51A(k) is 6–14 years — same bracket, reinforcing their symmetry.
• RTE Act 2009 came into force on 1 April 2010.
• The 86th Amendment also amended Article 45 (DPSP) — changing it from a directive to provide free education for children under 14 to early childhood care for children under 6.

solution.concept_anchor: Courts enforce Article 21 not FD directly — MC Mehta principle
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students aware that 51A(g) was used in MC Mehta cases may conclude the court enforced 51A(g) directly, missing the critical point that Article 21 was the actual enforcement vehicle.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — Article 51A(g) cannot be enforced by writ; courts use it as interpretive support, not as a direct enforcement basis.
Eliminate option (c) — PILs have been admitted in similar environmental cases; the court does not necessarily dismiss for lack of cause of action.

Retain option (b) — courts will admit the petition and enforce the right to a clean environment through Article 21, using 51A(g) as interpretive support, not as the primary enforcement basis.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap makes option (a) appealing by suggesting direct enforcement of 51A(g) — which the MC Mehta cases famously used. Students recall '51A(g) was used in MC Mehta' and conclude the court enforced 51A(g) directly. The precise knowledge required is that enforcement was through Article 21 (right to life interpreted to include a clean environment), with 51A(g) serving only as interpretive support.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the critical distinction between Fundamental Duties as interpretive tools versus direct enforcement provisions — the central lesson of the MC Mehta line of jurisprudence.

Applicable principle: Courts cannot enforce Fundamental Duties directly through writ petitions. However, PILs citing State inaction that causes FD-relevant harm (such as environmental degradation affecting Article 21 rights) are admitted and decided through Article 21/32, with FDs serving as interpretive and normative support.

• Option (a): Incorrect. No writ petition can be sustained on Article 51A(g) alone. The court cannot issue directions based solely on a Fundamental Duty — this has been consistently held.
• Option (b): Correct. The court will likely admit the PIL and frame relief under Article 21 (right to a clean and healthy environment), treating 51A(g) as a constitutional signal supporting the expansive reading of Article 21 — precisely the MC Mehta approach.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Courts have consistently admitted environmental PILs even where the primary grievance involves FD-related obligations — the cause of action is framed around Article 21 violation, not 51A(g) directly.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Article 48A (DPSP on environmental protection) is also non-justiciable and cannot independently ground a writ petition, though it strengthens the Article 21-based argument.

Value Addition:
• M.C. Mehta v. Union of India established that the right to live in a pollution-free environment is part of Article 21.
• Article 48A and Article 51A(g) together create a 'constitutional ecology' — both non-justiciable but mutually reinforcing.
• Supreme Court under Article 142 has issued sweeping environmental directions going beyond strict statutory frameworks.

concepts_used: Fundamental Duties Applicable Only to Citizens: Exclusion of Non-Citizens

solution.concept_anchor: Article 51A — every citizen, not every person
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because Article 20 (protection against double jeopardy and self-incrimination) is available to all 'persons', and students may incorrectly assume Fundamental Duties similarly cover all persons.
elimination_logic: Articles 14, 20, and 21 use the word 'person' — they extend to all persons including foreign nationals and legal entities.
Article 51A uses 'every citizen' — it applies exclusively to Indian citizens, excluding foreign nationals, corporations, and other legal persons.
The odd one out is Article 51A(g) — it is the only provision among the four that is restricted to 'every citizen' rather than 'every person'.
Correct answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the scope of Fundamental Rights (many of which protect 'persons') with Fundamental Duties (which protect only 'citizens'). Students who know Article 21 and Article 14 protect persons, and who also know that FDs are constitutional obligations, may not notice that the key distinction is in the subject of the obligation — 'person' vs. 'citizen'. Article 51A(g) is the only option among the four that does not protect or apply to 'every person'.
solution.final_explanation:
The Indian Constitution deliberately uses different terms — 'person' and 'citizen' — to determine the scope of constitutional provisions.

• Option (a) — Article 14 (Equality before law): Uses 'any person' — applies to all persons within Indian territory, including foreign nationals and legal entities.
• Option (b) — Article 20 (Protection against certain convictions): Uses 'any person' — extends to all persons, not limited to citizens.
• Option (c) — Article 51A(g) (FD to protect environment): Uses 'every citizen' — applies exclusively to Indian citizens. This is the odd one out, as it does not protect or apply to 'every person'.
• Option (d) — Article 21 (Protection of life and personal liberty): Uses 'any person' — universally applicable, not restricted to citizens.

Value Addition:
• Among Fundamental Rights, Articles 15, 16, 19, and 29–30 are citizen-specific — recognising this pattern prevents errors.
• All eleven Fundamental Duties apply only to citizens — no exception within Part IVA.
• The citizen-exclusivity of FDs means that even if FDs were made justiciable, foreign nationals and corporations would fall outside their ambit constitutionally.

concepts_used: Moral vs. Legal Enforceability: The Nature of Fundamental Duties as Constitutional Morality

solution.concept_anchor: Granville Austin — FDs as conscience of Constitution
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because Dr. B.R. Ambedkar is closely associated with constitutional morality and the Constitution generally, making him a plausible but incorrect attribution for this specific description of FDs.
elimination_logic: Eliminate Dr. B.R. Ambedkar — while Ambedkar articulated 'constitutional morality', the specific phrase 'conscience of the Constitution' describing FDs is attributed to Granville Austin, the constitutional historian.
Eliminate Jawaharlal Nehru — not associated with this characterisation of Fundamental Duties.
Eliminate Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar — a Constituent Assembly member not associated with this characterisation.
Retain Granville Austin — the constitutional historian who described Fundamental Duties as 'the conscience of the Constitution' emphasising their moral force without legal sanction.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes Dr. B.R. Ambedkar — who is legitimately associated with 'constitutional morality' as a concept — for Granville Austin, who specifically described FDs as 'the conscience of the Constitution'. Students conflate Ambedkar's broader constitutional morality framework with Austin's specific characterisation of FDs, selecting option (c) instead of (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Fundamental Duties represent what scholars call 'constitutional morality' — a normative civic framework codified without legal sanction.

• Option (a): Correct. Granville Austin, the American constitutional historian who wrote extensively on the Indian Constitution, described Fundamental Duties as 'the conscience of the Constitution' — emphasising their moral force as a normative standard without legal compulsion.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Jawaharlal Nehru, though deeply involved in framing the Constitution, is not attributed this specific characterisation of Fundamental Duties.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar articulated 'constitutional morality' as a broader concept distinct from public morality, but the specific phrase 'conscience of the Constitution' for FDs is Austin's coinage, not Ambedkar's.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar was a prominent Constituent Assembly member but is not attributed this description.

Value Addition:
• Austin's other notable phrase: he described the Indian Constitution as a 'seamless web' of three strands — democracy, socialism, and secularism.
• Ambedkar's 'constitutional morality' concept holds that constitutional norms must override popular/public morality.
• The moral force of FDs operates through civic education, social sanction, and peer pressure — the 'soft enforcement' mechanism envisioned by the Verma Committee.

solution.concept_anchor: Penal statutes implement FDs but derive power from legislative competence
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act is indeed linked to Article 51A(a) but students may incorrectly believe such laws derive enforcement power from Article 51A itself rather than from Parliament's ordinary legislative competence.
elimination_logic: Check option (a): The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971) does give effect to Article 51A(a) — but the enforcement power derives from Parliament's legislative competence, not from Article 51A. The pair description suggesting it derives power from Article 51A is incorrect.

Check option (b): The Wildlife Protection Act (1972) is correctly associated with Article 51A(g) (protect natural environment including wildlife) and the enforcement power derives from Parliament's legislative competence under the Union/Concurrent lists. This pair is correctly matched.
Check option (c): The RTE Act 2009 operationalises Article 21A (not Article 51A(k) as its primary constitutional anchor). The pair claiming 51A(k) as the enforcement source is imprecise.
Check option (d): There is no such provision in the Companies Act directly linked to Article 51A(h). Option (b) remains the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap makes option (a) attractive by correctly identifying the Act-FD connection but subtly misattributing the source of enforcement power. Students who know the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act implements Article 51A(a) may overlook the critical legal nuance — the enforcement power comes from legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule, not from Article 51A itself.
solution.final_explanation:
Several penal statutes give indirect effect to Fundamental Duties, but the source of their enforcement power is always Parliament's ordinary legislative competence, not Article 51A.

• Option (a): Incorrectly matched. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971) does implement Article 51A(a) in spirit, but the Act predates the 42nd Amendment (1976) — FDs provided retrospective constitutional backing, not the initial enforcement power. The stated enforcement source is incorrect.
• Option (b): Correctly matched. The Wildlife Protection Act (1972) aligns with Article 51A(g)'s mandate to protect the natural environment including forests and wildlife. The Act derives its enforcement power from Parliament's legislative competence (Concurrent List entries on forests and wildlife), not from Article 51A directly.
• Option (c): Incorrectly matched. The RTE Act 2009 is anchored primarily in Article 21A (Fundamental Right), not Article 51A(k) (which is non-justiciable). 51A(k) provides normative backing, not enforcement power.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched. CSR provisions under the Companies Act 2013 reflect the spirit of 51A(g), not 51A(h) (scientific temper). The pairing is fabricated.

Value Addition:
• Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971 was enacted before FDs — constitutional backing came retrospectively in 1976.
• Wildlife Protection Act 1972 and Environment Protection Act 1986 are the two major environmental laws with FD backing.
• Laws implementing FDs must still conform to Fundamental Rights — constitutional backing does not confer immunity from challenge.

concepts_used: Comparison with Fundamental Duties in Other Constitutions: USSR, Japan, Germany

solution.concept_anchor: India chose non-justiciability unlike USSR model — deliberate choice

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Fundamental Duties were inspired by the USSR Constitution, which contained justiciable duties unlike the non-justiciable duties India adopted.
statement_analysis.reason: India's FDs drew inspiration from the Soviet constitutional model (1936/1977), where duties were backed by legal enforcement — India consciously chose to depart from this by making FDs non-justiciable.

statement_analysis.statement: Germany's Basic Law contains explicit and fully enforceable Fundamental Duties covering a wide range of civic obligations, making it the most comprehensive duty-enforcement model among constitutional democracies.
statement_analysis.reason: Germany's Basic Law contains limited implied duties; the most notable is Article 14(2) — 'property entails obligations' (social obligation of property) — which is not a comprehensive civic duty framework and is not fully analogous to India's FDs.

statement_analysis.statement: Japan's Constitution includes duties of education, work, and tax payment, which are partially enforceable — distinguishing it from India where all Fundamental Duties are uniformly non-justiciable.
statement_analysis.reason: Japan's constitutional duties (education, work, taxation) have varying degrees of enforceability — partially enforceable — unlike India's uniform non-justiciable approach.

statement_analysis.statement: India's decision to adopt non-justiciable Fundamental Duties despite being inspired by the justiciable USSR model represents a deliberate constitutional choice, not an oversight by the framers.
statement_analysis.reason: The Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation for enforcement was rejected — the departure from the USSR model was a deliberate political and constitutional decision, reflecting concerns about imposing legal obligations on citizens in a democracy.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' is correct and 'Only two' is a strong distractor because Statement 2's false claim about Germany sounds authoritative and students unfamiliar with the German Basic Law's limited duty framework may accept it, reducing the count to two.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: USSR model is the acknowledged inspiration for Indian FDs, and the USSR had justiciable duties — Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2: Germany's Basic Law does not have a 'comprehensive' FD framework — Article 14(2) is the primary social obligation clause, limited to property. 'Most comprehensive model' is an overstatement; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Japan's duties of education, work, and taxation are partially enforceable — correct.
Verify Statement 4: The deliberate rejection of the Swaran Singh Committee's enforceability recommendation confirms intentionality — correct.
Three statements correct (1, 3, 4), one incorrect (2) — answer is (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in Statement 2 overstates Germany's duty framework by attributing to it a 'comprehensive' and 'fully enforceable' duty system. Students who know Germany has some constitutional duties (Article 14(2) is a real provision) may accept the exaggerated characterisation without questioning the scope claim, thereby falsely marking Statement 2 as correct and selecting 'All four' instead of 'Only three'.
solution.final_explanation:
India's comparative constitutional choice on FD enforceability is a significant UPSC theme — particularly the departure from the USSR model.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The USSR Constitution (1936, reaffirmed 1977) was the primary inspiration for Indian FDs. Soviet duties were justiciable — India adopted the concept but deliberately removed the enforcement mechanism.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Germany's Basic Law does not contain a comprehensive FD framework. Its most notable duty-related provision is Article 14(2): 'Property entails obligations; its use shall also serve the public good.' This is an implied social obligation on property rights, not a broad civic duty system comparable to India's or the USSR's.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Japan's Constitution Article 26 (education), Article 27 (work), and Article 30 (taxation) impose partially enforceable duties — for example, tax obligations are legally enforceable while education duties are more aspirational.
• Statement 4 — Correct: India's non-justiciability was a deliberate choice — the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation for penal enforcement was rejected, confirming intentionality rather than constitutional inadvertence.

Value Addition:
• The USSR 1977 Constitution (Brezhnev Constitution) is specifically mentioned in Swaran Singh Committee discussions as the inspiration.
• India is among the few democracies to list FDs without any enforcement mechanism — most constitutional democracies either enforce duties or do not list them.
• The deliberate choice reflects the 'rights-centric' philosophical orientation of the Indian constitutional framework.

concepts_used: Fundamental Duties and Judicial Activism: Expanding Enforcement through PIL and Article 21

solution.concept_anchor: Article 21 — judicial enforcement vehicle, not Article 51A
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Courts have expanded Article 21 to encompass State obligations that mirror citizens' FDs — for example, the right to a clean environment, derived from FD 51A(g), has been read into Article 21.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. There is no provision in the Constitution that makes Fundamental Duties directly justiciable or that converts citizen duties into State obligations as a constitutional rule. R is a fabricated legal mechanism — the judicial creativity operates through Article 21/32, not through any provision converting FDs into State obligations.
Step 3: Since R is incorrect, the answer is (c) — A correct, R incorrect.
Correct option is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap makes R sound like a plausible constitutional mechanism — 'citizens' duties become State obligations' sounds like a logical judicial doctrine. Students familiar with the MC Mehta expansion may accept this as the stated constitutional basis, not recognising it as a fabricated provision. The actual mechanism is purely judicial interpretation of Article 21 — not any constitutional rule converting FDs into State duties.
solution.final_explanation:
The MC Mehta line of cases demonstrates the Supreme Court's creative use of Article 21 to expand constitutional obligations — but the mechanism is purely interpretive, not based on any provision that converts citizen duties into State obligations.

Assertion (A): Correct. Through expansive interpretation of Article 21 (right to life), courts have recognised rights that mirror citizens' FDs — particularly the right to a clean environment (mirroring 51A(g)), right to education (mirroring 51A(k)), and right to a pollution-free atmosphere. The State is then directed to create conditions for citizens to fulfill these duties.

Reason (R): Incorrect. There is no constitutional provision that converts citizens' Fundamental Duties into enforceable State obligations. R describes a mechanism that does not exist in constitutional text. The judicial expansion operates through Article 21's generous interpretation — courts use FDs as contextual support for expanding Article 21's scope, not through any duty-conversion mechanism.

Since A is correct and R is incorrect, the correct option is (c).

Value Addition:
• M.C. Mehta v. Union of India series (Oleum Gas Leak, Ganga Pollution, Vehicular Pollution cases) are the primary examples of FD-informed Article 21 expansion.
• Article 142 has also been used by the SC to issue comprehensive environmental directions beyond statutory frameworks.
• The SC's approach effectively creates State obligations corresponding to citizen duties — but through judicial interpretation, not constitutional mandate.

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment adds FDs; 44th Amendment retains them
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because students who know FDs were added during the Emergency era may confuse the 42nd and 44th Amendments' sequence, and some may believe the 44th Amendment added FDs (since it reversed other 42nd Amendment provisions).
elimination_logic: Anchor: The original Constitution (1950) had no Fundamental Duties — this is the starting point.
The Swaran Singh Committee submitted recommendations in 1976, which formed the basis for the 42nd Amendment (1976) — this added the first 10 FDs.
The 44th Amendment (1978) came after the Emergency ended and repealed several 42nd Amendment provisions but retained FDs — confirming political consensus on their inclusion.
The 86th Amendment (2002) added the 11th FD under Article 51A(k) — the final event in the sequence.

Correct order: Original Constitution (no FDs) → Swaran Singh Committee (1976) → 42nd Amendment adding 10 FDs (1976) → 44th Amendment retaining FDs (1978) → 86th Amendment adding 11th FD (2002). Option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap confuses the roles of the 42nd and 44th Amendments. Students know the 44th Amendment reversed several Emergency-era provisions and may assume it was the 44th Amendment that added FDs (as a post-Emergency corrective) rather than the 42nd. The precise knowledge required: FDs were added by the 42nd Amendment during the Emergency; the 44th Amendment retained FDs while removing other controversial Emergency provisions.
solution.final_explanation:
The chronological history of Fundamental Duties spans nearly five decades and involves four distinct constitutional events.

Correct sequence: The original Constitution of 1950 contained no Fundamental Duties — this was a deliberate omission by the Constituent Assembly. The Swaran Singh Committee's 1976 recommendations led directly to the 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976), which inserted Part IVA with ten Fundamental Duties during the Emergency period. After the Emergency ended, the 44th Amendment (1978) repealed several controversial changes made by the 42nd Amendment but explicitly retained Fundamental Duties — evidence of bipartisan consensus on their inclusion. Finally, the 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) added the eleventh duty under Article 51A(k) — the parent/guardian duty — paired with the insertion of Article 21A.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (b): Placing the 44th Amendment before the 42nd is factually impossible — the 44th responded to the 42nd.
• Option (c): Placing the 86th Amendment before the 44th reverses a 24-year gap.
• Option (d): Any sequence starting with the 86th Amendment is chronologically absurd.

Value Addition:
• Critics questioned the legitimacy of FDs added during Emergency when democratic processes were suspended.
• The 44th Amendment's retention of FDs is taken as evidence that FDs enjoy broader constitutional consensus than other Emergency-era additions.
• India initially had no list of FDs — unlike the USSR, which served as inspiration and had duties from the start.

concepts_used: Fundamental Duty 51A(f): Valuing Composite Culture and its Enforceability Challenges

solution.concept_anchor: Aspirational FDs vs. FDs with indirect penal enforcement

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(f), which requires citizens to value and preserve the rich heritage of India's composite culture, is among the most difficult Fundamental Duties to enforce legally because its content is inherently subjective and requires social transformation rather than legal compulsion.
statement_analysis.reason: The duty to 'value and preserve composite culture' involves normative judgments about cultural identity — what constitutes 'composite culture' and how to 'value' it cannot be objectively determined or legally mandated, making it inherently aspirational and legally unenforceable.

statement_analysis.statement: All eleven Fundamental Duties are equally unenforceable in practice because none has any corresponding penal statute or indirect legal mechanism giving effect to it.
statement_analysis.reason: This is an overstatement — FDs like 51A(a) (respect national symbols) and 51A(g) (protect environment) have corresponding penal statutes (Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act and Wildlife Protection Act) that give them indirect enforcement. Not all FDs are equally unenforceable.

statement_analysis.statement: The inherent unenforceability of aspirational Fundamental Duties such as Article 51A(b) (cherishing noble ideals of the freedom struggle) illustrates why the framers of Part IVA chose a moral rather than a legal framework for citizen obligations.
statement_analysis.reason: Duties like 51A(b) and 51A(f) are aspirational and inspirational — their content cannot be legally defined or compelled. Their inclusion reflects a choice to codify civic morality rather than legal obligation, reinforcing the non-justiciable character of the entire FD framework.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) is a strong distractor because statements 1 and 3 are clearly correct, and students who accept Statement 2's 'none has any corresponding law' claim without critical evaluation will mark all three as correct.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — 'value and preserve composite culture' is subjective and aspirational; legal enforcement is structurally impossible. Correct.

Scrutinise Statement 2 — 'none has any corresponding penal statute' is directly contradicted by the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (51A(a)) and Wildlife Protection Act (51A(g)). Statement 2 is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3 — aspirational duties like 51A(b) and 51A(f) exemplify the moral rather than legal character of the FD framework. Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (b) 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 uses the word 'all' and 'none' — absolute qualifiers that make an otherwise partially true claim false. It is true that many FDs lack enforcement statutes, but the absolute claim (none has any) is false because specific FDs like 51A(a) and 51A(g) do have indirect penal enforcement through existing legislation. Students who remember the general non-justiciability of FDs may accept the 'none' qualifier without checking specific exceptions.
solution.final_explanation:
Fundamental Duties vary significantly in their amenability to enforcement — some are purely aspirational while others have corresponding penal statutes.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 51A(f)'s mandate to 'value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture' is inherently subjective. 'Composite culture' itself is a contested concept, and 'valuing' it is a matter of personal disposition rather than legal conduct. No penal statute could objectively define a violation of this duty.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The absolute claim that 'none' of the FDs has a corresponding enforcement mechanism is false. Article 51A(a) (respect national symbols) is implemented through the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971); Article 51A(g) (protect environment) is implemented through the Wildlife Protection Act (1972) and Environmental Protection Act (1986).
• Statement 3 — Correct: Duties like Article 51A(b) (cherish freedom struggle ideals) and 51A(f) (preserve composite culture) are aspirational by design — they express civic virtues that cannot be legally compelled, illustrating the framers' choice of moral over legal obligation.

Value Addition:
• The spectrum of FD enforceability: fully aspirational (51A(b),(f),(h)) → indirectly enforced (51A(a),(g)) → paired with enforceable right (51A(k)).
• Verma Committee (1999) acknowledged this spectrum in its report.
• 51A(h) — developing scientific temper — is also aspirational but is addressed through educational curricula under NCF.

concepts_used: Fundamental Duties and Corporate/Institutional Liability: Applicability Debate

solution.concept_anchor: Corporations excluded from FDs; legislation can impose equivalent duties

statement_analysis.statement: Since Article 51A uses the phrase 'every citizen', corporations and other legal persons are constitutionally excluded from the direct application of Fundamental Duties, though Parliament can enact legislation imposing equivalent obligations on them.
statement_analysis.reason: FDs apply only to natural persons who are Indian citizens. Corporations are legal persons, not citizens, and are excluded from direct FD applicability. However, Parliament's legislative competence allows it to impose equivalent statutory duties on corporations — as with the Companies Act 2013's CSR provisions.

statement_analysis.statement: Courts cannot impose any FD-like obligation on corporations even through judicial directions under Article 142, since Article 142 can only be invoked to enforce constitutional provisions that directly apply to the entity in question.
statement_analysis.reason: Courts have used Article 142 to issue comprehensive directions imposing environmental and cultural preservation obligations on corporations — even though FDs do not directly apply to them. Article 142 is not limited to enforcing provisions that directly apply to the respondent; it allows courts to do 'complete justice' in any pending matter.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is correct and students may accept Statement 2 as a logical extension of the rule that FDs don't apply to corporations, without recognising Article 142's expansive scope.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is constitutionally accurate — 'every citizen' excludes corporations; Parliament can legislate equivalent duties. Mark correct.

Statement 2 contains an overstatement about Article 142 — courts have used Article 142 to impose FD-like environmental obligations on corporations even when FDs don't directly apply. Article 142 is not limited to provisions directly applicable to the respondent. Mark incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 makes a plausible-sounding limitation on Article 142 — that it can only enforce provisions directly applicable to the respondent. This sounds logical (FDs don't apply to corporations, so courts can't use Article 142 for FD-like obligations). But Article 142's 'complete justice' mandate is extremely broad, and courts have used it creatively to impose obligations on corporations in environmental and public interest matters regardless of direct constitutional applicability.
solution.final_explanation:
The corporate applicability of Fundamental Duties raises important questions about enforcement mechanisms at the intersection of constitutional text and judicial creativity.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 51A's 'every citizen' language is clear — corporations are legal persons, not citizens, and are categorically excluded from the direct application of Fundamental Duties. However, this does not prevent Parliament from enacting legislation (such as CSR provisions under Companies Act 2013) that imposes equivalent obligations on corporations through its ordinary legislative power.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 142 grants the Supreme Court power to pass any order necessary to do 'complete justice' in any matter pending before it. Courts have invoked this to impose comprehensive environmental obligations on corporations — obligations that mirror FD 51A(g) — even though FDs do not constitutionally bind corporations. Article 142 is not constrained to provisions directly applicable to the respondent party.

Value Addition:
• Article 142 has been described as the 'residual plenary power' of the Supreme Court — extremely broad and not limited to constitutional provisions directly applicable to parties.
• Companies Act 2013, Section 135 (CSR) — 2% of average net profit for eligible companies — reflects the spirit of 51A(g) and 51A(h) through statutory rather than constitutional compulsion.
• The SEBI and NGT have also imposed environmental obligations on corporations through regulatory frameworks aligned with FD 51A(g)'s spirit.

solution.concept_anchor: Correlative theory — jurisprudential argument, not settled law
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because students aware of the correlative theory and its academic acceptance may assume it has been declared settled law by a Constitution Bench, rather than remaining a jurisprudential argument.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — the correlative theory does not make FDs enforceable under Article 32; courts have consistently rejected writ petitions based solely on FDs.

Eliminate option (c) — while SC judgments have endorsed the correlative theory (Chandra Bhavan Boarding), it has NOT been declared settled constitutional law by a Constitution Bench. FDs remain non-justiciable.
Eliminate option (d) — the theory is not 'purely academic'; it has been cited in SC judgments and by constitutional commissions.
Retain option (b) — the correlative theory remains a jurisprudential argument used in interpretation but has not altered the settled non-justiciability of FDs.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap in option (c) creates a believable judicial authority — 'declared settled constitutional law by a Constitution Bench'. Students who know the SC has endorsed the correlative theory in judgments may assume a formal Constitution Bench declaration exists. The precise knowledge required is that no such definitive ruling has elevated the correlative theory to the status of settled law — FDs remain non-justiciable despite judicial endorsement of the theory's logic.
solution.final_explanation:
The correlative theory posits that rights and duties are inseparable in a democratic framework — if citizens have rights, they must also have duties, and violations of duties should carry consequences similar to violations of rights.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The correlative theory does not create a basis for enforcing FDs under Article 32. Courts have consistently held that no writ petition can be sustained on a Fundamental Duty alone — the correlative theory influences interpretation, not enforcement.
• Option (b): Correct. The correlative theory remains a jurisprudential argument — endorsed in judgments like Chandra Bhavan Boarding v. State of Mysore and cited by the H.J. Kenia Committee (1974) — but it has not altered the non-justiciable status of FDs. It is used interpretively, not as an enforcement mechanism.
• Option (c): Incorrect. No Constitution Bench has declared the correlative theory as settled constitutional law requiring FD enforceability. This is a fabricated judicial authority.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The theory is not purely academic — it has been cited in SC judgments and constitutional commission reports, giving it real (if limited) legal relevance.

Value Addition:
• H.J. Kenia Committee (1974) predates the 42nd Amendment and first articulated the correlative rights-duties framework in India.
• Chandra Bhavan Boarding v. State of Mysore is the key SC judgment endorsing the inseparability of rights and duties.
• The correlative theory is strongest as an argument for future constitutional reform rather than as current enforcement jurisprudence.

solution.concept_anchor: FD violations → penal law → RPA disqualification: indirect chain

statement_analysis.statement: Violation of a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A can directly disqualify a person from contesting elections under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, since FDs are constitutional obligations whose breach carries electoral consequences.
statement_analysis.reason: Fundamental Duties do not directly cause electoral disqualification. The indirect chain is: FD violation → conviction under an implementing penal statute (e.g., Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act) → Section 8 RPA disqualification. The FD itself is not the trigger for disqualification.

statement_analysis.statement: A person convicted under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 — which gives effect to Article 51A(a) — may face electoral disqualification under Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, provided the conviction carries the requisite sentence.
statement_analysis.reason: This correctly describes the indirect enforcement chain — conviction under an FD-implementing penal statute can lead to RPA disqualification if the sentence threshold under Section 8 is met. This is an indirect, not direct, consequence of FD-related conduct.

statement_analysis.statement: Since Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, no law enacted by Parliament can use FD violation as the basis for any legal consequence, including criminal prosecution, civil liability, or electoral disqualification.
statement_analysis.reason: This overstates non-justiciability. Parliament can and has enacted penal statutes implementing FDs (Wildlife Protection Act, Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act) — these laws impose criminal liability for conduct that also violates FDs. Non-justiciability means no direct writ enforcement; it does not prevent Parliament from legislating consequences.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (2 only) is a strong distractor because Statement 2 is the only correct statement, and students who correctly identify it as correct may choose (b) — but the question asks for statements that are NOT correct, making (c) [1 and 3] the answer.
elimination_logic: Read the stem carefully — the question asks which statements are NOT correct.
Statement 1: The claim of 'direct' disqualification is false — the mechanism is indirect through penal conviction. NOT correct.
Statement 2: The indirect chain (conviction under implementing statute → Section 8 RPA disqualification) is accurately described. This IS correct.
Statement 3: The absolute claim that 'no law can use FD violation as basis for legal consequence' is false — Parliament has enacted penal statutes implementing FDs. NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1's partial-truth trap correctly identifies the connection between FD violations and electoral disqualification but falsely characterises it as 'direct'. Students who know FD violations can lead to disqualification (true in an indirect sense) may mark Statement 1 as correct without noticing the 'directly' qualifier that makes it incorrect. The distinction between direct constitutional disqualification and indirect statutory disqualification through a penal conviction chain is the critical knowledge point.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between Fundamental Duties and electoral law operates through an indirect chain involving penal statutes — not through any direct constitutional disqualification provision.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: FDs do not directly trigger electoral disqualification under the RPA 1951. The indirect chain is: FD-violating conduct → conviction under an implementing statute (e.g., Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act) → Section 8 RPA disqualification if the sentence threshold is met. No constitutional provision makes FD violation itself a ground for disqualification.
• Statement 2 — Correct: This accurately describes the operative mechanism. Conviction under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (which implements Article 51A(a)) can attract Section 8 RPA disqualification if the punishment meets the threshold — an indirect but real electoral consequence of FD-related conduct.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: Non-justiciability means FDs cannot be directly enforced by writ — it does not prevent Parliament from enacting legislation that makes FD-violating conduct criminal or legally consequential. The Wildlife Protection Act and Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act demonstrate Parliament's capacity to legislate legal consequences for FD-related conduct.

Value Addition:
• Section 8 RPA 1951 disqualifies persons convicted of specified offences or sentenced to two or more years' imprisonment.
• Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971 — offences under it can carry imprisonment, potentially triggering Section 8 disqualification.
• Non-justiciability is a structural feature (no direct writ enforcement), not a blanket immunity from all legal consequences.

solution.concept_anchor: FDs vs DPSPs — non-justiciable but legally distinct

statement_analysis.statement: Both Directive Principles of State Policy and Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, meaning neither can be directly enforced by courts through writ jurisdiction.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the foundational similarity — both Part IV (DPSPs) and Part IVA (FDs) lack enforcement clauses and cannot be directly enforced through writ petitions under Articles 32 or 226.

statement_analysis.statement: Directive Principles of State Policy and Fundamental Duties are identical in their legal character because both are merely 'aspirational' provisions with no legal effect whatsoever on judicial proceedings.
statement_analysis.reason: While both are non-justiciable, they differ significantly in legal character. DPSPs can be used to justify restrictions on Fundamental Rights (Article 31C) and to guide legislative policy. FDs are used as interpretive tools. Neither is legally irrelevant — calling them identical mischaracterises both.

statement_analysis.statement: DPSPs impose obligations on the State while Fundamental Duties impose obligations on citizens — this difference in the subject of obligation is the primary structural distinction between the two.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the defining structural distinction. DPSPs are instructions to the State in governance; FDs are instructions to citizens in civic life. Both are non-justiciable but the obligation-bearer is categorically different.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 31C of the Constitution gives special protection to laws enacted to implement Directive Principles of State Policy, and a similar constitutional provision grants equivalent protection to laws enacted to implement Fundamental Duties.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 31C protects laws implementing specified DPSPs from challenge under Articles 14 and 19. There is no equivalent provision in the Constitution protecting laws implementing Fundamental Duties — this is a fabricated parallel that does not exist in constitutional text.

solution.strong_distractor: b — 'Only two' is the correct answer; 'Only three' is the strong distractor for students who accept Statement 2's conflation of DPSPs and FDs as 'identical and merely aspirational' or Statement 4's fabricated Article 31C parallel.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Both DPSPs and FDs are non-justiciable by writ — unambiguously correct.

Statement 2: DPSPs and FDs are NOT identical in legal character — DPSPs inform Article 31C protection and legislative guidance; FDs serve as interpretive tools. The 'no legal effect' claim is false. Incorrect.
Statement 3: DPSPs → State obligations; FDs → citizen obligations. This structural distinction is correct.
Statement 4: Article 31C exists for DPSPs but no equivalent provision exists for FDs — the fabricated parallel makes Statement 4 incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statements 2 and 4 incorrect — only two correct. Answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 deploys a plausible-fabrication trap by creating an 'Article 31C equivalent for FDs' that sounds like a logical constitutional symmetry but does not exist. Students familiar with Article 31C and aware that laws implementing FDs also get 'constitutional backing' may conflate 'constitutional backing' with Article 31C-type protection, selecting three correct statements instead of two.
solution.final_explanation:
Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties share non-justiciability but differ significantly in other legal dimensions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The shared non-justiciability of DPSPs and FDs is their most commonly tested similarity — neither can be directly enforced through writ petitions under Articles 32 or 226.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Non-justiciability does not mean 'no legal effect'. DPSPs guide legislative policy, inform Article 31C protection, and can justify reasonable restrictions on FRs. FDs serve as interpretive tools for courts. Describing both as 'mere aspirational provisions with no legal effect' mischaracterises the legal significance courts have accorded to both.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The obligation-bearer distinction is the primary structural difference. DPSPs are policy mandates directed at the State; FDs are civic obligations directed at individual citizens.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Article 31C provides that laws implementing specified DPSPs cannot be challenged under Articles 14 or 19. No equivalent provision exists for laws implementing Fundamental Duties — the fabricated symmetry does not exist in the constitutional text.

Value Addition:
• Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971) and modified by the 44th Amendment.
• Kesavananda Bharati case limited Article 31C's scope — only specified DPSPs (Articles 39(b) and 39(c)) enjoy this protection after the 44th Amendment.
• Laws implementing FDs must still conform to Part III — no Article 31C-type immunity shields them from FR challenge.

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment added FDs; 44th Amendment retained them
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The 44th Amendment (1978) did retain Fundamental Duties despite repealing several other 42nd Amendment provisions. This is factually accurate and widely accepted as evidence of bipartisan consensus.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The original Constitution of 1950 contained no Fundamental Duties — they were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 during the Emergency. This is factually accurate.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The fact that FDs were Emergency additions (R) is precisely the context that makes the 44th Amendment's retention significant (A) — if they were Emergency impositions lacking legitimacy, the post-Emergency 44th Amendment would have removed them. Their retention despite this origin demonstrates bipartisan consensus, which is what A asserts. R provides the essential backdrop that gives A its meaning.
Both A and R correct, and R explains A — correct option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap makes option (b) tempting — both A and R are correct, and students who reflexively avoid option (a) in assertion-reason questions (suspecting traps) may choose (b). The precise reasoning required is recognising that R genuinely explains A: the Emergency-era origin of FDs (R) is the very context that makes the 44th Amendment's retention significant as evidence of consensus (A). R is not merely an adjacent fact — it is the causal backdrop for the significance of A.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional history of Fundamental Duties involves a significant legitimacy question — their Emergency-era origin — which the 44th Amendment's retention directly addresses.

Assertion (A): Correct. When the Janata government enacted the 44th Amendment (1978) after the Emergency ended, it repealed several controversial 42nd Amendment provisions — including changes to Article 352 and other emergency provisions. However, it retained Fundamental Duties. This is widely interpreted as reflecting bipartisan acceptance that FDs had value independent of their Emergency-era origins.

Reason (R): Correct. The original Constitution of India (1950), as drafted by the Constituent Assembly, contained no Fundamental Duties. The Constituent Assembly did not include any equivalent of Part IVA. Fundamental Duties were added entirely by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) during the Emergency period under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's government.

Causal Relationship: R genuinely explains A. The Emergency-era, non-Constituent Assembly origin of FDs (R) is precisely the context that makes the 44th Amendment's retention of FDs (A) significant as evidence of bipartisan consensus — a post-Emergency government chose not to repeal them, implying they had merit beyond Emergency politics.

Value Addition:
• 42nd Amendment (1976) is the most sweeping constitutional amendment — sometimes called the 'mini-Constitution'.
• 44th Amendment (1978) reversed provisions on preventive detention, emergency proclamation, and judicial review curtailment but left FDs intact.
• Critics argue FDs lack the legitimacy of Constituent Assembly deliberation — the 44th Amendment's retention is the standard counter-argument.
